features.title: Original art. Twice the detail.
features.intro: 2× terrain and feature sprites, synthesized from the game’s own artwork.
features.original: Map tiles are 32 × 32 pixels, and trees and other sprite features have fixed-resolution artwork. Enlarging them directly makes each source pixel a larger block.
features.how: The detail view builds 64 × 64 terrain tiles and 2× feature sprites using patch matching against the original art and its palette blends. Results are cached locally. This is texture synthesis from your game data, not newly drawn replacement art.
features.look: the individual grass pixels, rock edges and tree canopy. The default 4× inspection magnifies the same captures so the extra synthesized detail is easier to see.
features.caption: Greenhaven · no units · 4× pixel inspection. The 2× game view is magnified another 2×; the camera itself reaches 2×.
features.capture: A staged camera view of unmodified Greenhaven terrain and placed foliage, with zero units and zero model draw packets. Both views use the same 2× camera. Only the synthesized terrain and sprite detail changes. The 4× inspection enlarges both captured images equally with nearest-neighbor presentation, centered on the rocks and tree canopy. It is a pixel inspection, not a new 4× game-camera mode; use 2× view to see the complete original framing.
features.altBefore: Greenhaven grass, rocks and trees at 2× zoom with original-resolution terrain and sprite artwork.
features.altAfter: The same empty Greenhaven clearing with 2× synthesized terrain and tree sprites.

features.title: Get closer to the action.
features.intro: A true 2× camera view, including freshly rendered units.
features.original: The retail battlefield has a fixed close view. Magnifying a finished image enlarges the same pixels.
features.how: Nanolathe’s camera moves between a tactical overview, the native view and 2× detail. At 2×, model geometry is rasterized at the output scale, so units, moving parts and silhouettes gain real screen detail alongside the higher-resolution terrain.
features.look: the Commander, factory and solar panels gaining detail as the camera moves in.
features.capture: A staged 12-unit outpost uses original models and frozen, activated COB poses. Every frame is freshly rendered at its camera scale, progressing from 1× to 2× at 30 frames per second. Unit locations stay fixed; this demonstrates the camera, rather than a running battle.

motion.label: Camera zooms from 1× to 2× over a Greenhaven outpost
motion.caption: Greenhaven · 5 seconds · actual camera zoom from 1× to 2×.

features.title: Read the whole battle.
features.intro: Pull back to an overview with icons that stay legible.
features.original: The minimap gives a broad picture, while detailed unit models belong to the main battlefield view.
features.how: At tactical scale, the modern renderer replaces tiny models with clear role and movement-family icons. Team colors identify ownership; category symbols help distinguish constructors, combat units and infrastructure. The 0.25× overview is one of the camera’s standard zoom stops.
features.look: the base becoming a cluster of infrastructure icons, with allied and opposing squads separated by the terrain.
features.capture: A staged 38-unit layout includes a base, a detached utility site, staggered allied squads and an opposing outpost. The real camera pulls back from 1× to 0.25×; the renderer introduces tactical icons at its normal threshold. Original models and active COB poses stay at fixed world locations throughout. Fog is omitted to show both sides.

motion.label: Camera pulls back from a Greenhaven base to tactical icons for two opposing forces
motion.caption: Greenhaven · 5 seconds · 1× battlefield view to 0.25× tactical overview.

features.title: Smoother edges. On every unit.
features.intro: Full-unit SSAA keeps small silhouettes and moving parts readable.
features.original: Retail anti-aliasing supersamples structures; mobile units and some live parts stay at native resolution. Its palette-based resolve can leave colored fringes.
features.how: With Anti-Alias enabled, the modern path rasterizes model subjects at twice the resolution in each direction. Four coverage samples resolve into each output pixel, blending edges with the actual scene beneath. Mobile units, live pieces and construction geometry benefit too.
features.look: the mobile units’ diagonal armor and gun barrels. The Annihilator building is included because classic anti-aliasing already treats structures; the GPU extends coverage to the moving army.
features.caption: Four mobile units & one building · CPU / GPU · 1× camera, magnified 4× for pixel inspection.
features.capture: Bulldog, Maverick, Zeus and Merl mobile units beside an Annihilator building. Both paths receive the same committed poses and camera, with Anti-Alias enabled. Classic pixels come from the indexed CPU framebuffer; modern pixels come from GPU geometry with full-unit SSAA. The 480 × 320 native 1× captures share a 240 × 160 crop at (120,70), enlarged 4× with nearest-neighbor sampling. This compares whole rendering paths, including their existing raster and compositing differences.
features.altBefore: Four mobile units and an Annihilator building in Nanolathe’s classic CPU renderer, enlarged to inspect individual pixels.
features.altAfter: The matching five units in Nanolathe’s modern GPU renderer with full-unit SSAA.

features.title: Light reaches the armor.
features.intro: A nearby blast lights model surfaces. Add glow to see its halo too.
features.original: Units have directional shading and explosions have bright palette art and flashes. Nearby blasts do not add this dynamic colored surface light or soft bloom.
features.how: Visible explosions and nanolathe particles provide light sources. Nearby model faces receive color according to distance and face direction, and smoke can catch that light. A separate emission layer gathers bright beams and effect pixels; blurred copies blend back into the scene as a soft halo.
features.look: the Bulldog’s right-hand armor brightening beside the explosion. GPU lighting isolates the surface light; GPU + glow adds bloom. Pause and switch at the same instant.
features.capture: An ARM Jeffy self-destructs beside a surviving Bulldog in a normal Great Divide session. Classic frames use the CPU indexed framebuffer; GPU frames use the same committed scene with dynamic lighting. Blast distortion, tree heat, wreck cooling, metallic glints and water effects are disabled. Bloom is off in the primary GPU view and enabled only in GPU + glow. Both native 1× views use the same 240 × 160 crop, enlarged 4× for inspection. The clip runs five seconds at normal simulation timing.

motion.label: Classic CPU and modern GPU views of an explosion illuminating a nearby Bulldog
motion.caption: Same explosion · Classic CPU / GPU lighting · distortion disabled in every view.

features.title: Feel the shockwave.
features.intro: An expanding distortion ring pushes through the image around a blast.
features.original: Explosion art, flashes and debris convey impact. The surrounding scene does not have this added refractive ring.
features.how: Large explosion events drive a short-lived expanding ring. A shader samples a copy of the world with a radial offset, displacing the image around the blast before fading away. Its age follows the recorded event, so pausing freezes the ring.
features.look: the grass and tree silhouettes bending outward around the single unit’s explosion. Replay to follow the short-lived rings.
features.capture: One visible ARM Bulldog is destroyed through its normal self-destruct damage path. Its authored BIG_UNIT explosion produces real debris and three short-lived renderer shockwaves. The simulation advances normally; the paired frames differ only in blast distortion. Five seconds at 30 frames per second, with the death triggered at one second.

motion.label: One Bulldog explodes and sends refractive shockwaves across the surrounding terrain
motion.caption: Great Divide · one unit self-destructs after 1 second · 5-second loop.

features.title: The air above fire shimmers.
features.intro: Burning vegetation sends a subtle heat haze into the view above it.
features.original: Burning trees already have fire and smoke animations. The background above them stays optically still.
features.how: Burning sprite features mark a rising plume in the modern renderer. A time-driven shader gently offsets the background inside it, with soft edges and lateral drift. The current implementation targets burning vegetation; it does not add a plume to every flame.
features.look: the terrain just above the three burning trees. The fire and smoke are identical; switching heat reveals the background shimmer.
features.capture: Three original architree01 features are placed in a clearing and ignited through the normal feature lifecycle one second into capture. Fire animation, smoke and three heat plumes advance with the real simulation. No units are in view. Both renders share each recorded state and differ only in tree heat distortion.

motion.label: Three trees ignite, with rising smoke and heat shimmer above the flames
motion.caption: Great Divide · three burning trees · current integrated heat effect · 5-second loop.

features.title: Smoldering wrecks cool down.
features.intro: Fresh wreckage glows with residual heat, then settles back into cold metal.
features.original: Destroyed units leave their original wreck models, without this temporary cooling glow and refractive heat plume.
features.how: A newly created wreck carries its birth time into the modern renderer. Its original texture warms through pale orange and red, cooling back to normal over six seconds. A weaker heat shimmer fades over ten seconds. The effect follows the wreck’s age and visibility, and disappears when it is reclaimed.
features.look: the crumpled metal losing its orange-red glow, and the background wavering above it. The final seconds show the cold wreck remaining after both effects have faded.
features.capture: An ARM Stumpy takes ordinary damage and dies through its normal COB death sequence in a Great Divide clearing. The session creates the real armstump_dead corpse at tick 120; no wreck age or birth metadata is invented. Paired renders of each committed frame retain or suppress that known birth time in presentation only. Blast distortion, bloom, battle lighting, material finishes and scorch are disabled to isolate the wreck. The native 2× camera renders 480 × 320; both views use the same 240 × 160 crop enlarged 4× with nearest-neighbor sampling. Thirteen seconds at normal speed include two seconds after the heat plume expires.

motion.label: A destroyed Stumpy leaves glowing wreckage that cools, with heat shimmer fading above it
motion.caption: One real Stumpy wreck · cooling glow and heat shimmer · 13 seconds · magnified pixel crop.

features.title: Water follows the wind.
features.intro: Quiet surface movement and soft shorelines bring coasts to life.
features.original: Water is painted into the terrain. Unit scripts add their original blue and white wake particles.
features.how: The modern renderer uses the map’s water mask and committed wind to move two irregular wave layers. Filtering the wind keeps changes gradual. Soft shoreline and water-building foam anchor the moving surface to the coast; the original script wakes remain.
features.look: the waves crossing the open water and the soft foam tracing the shoreline. There are no units or wakes in this example.
features.capture: A newly recorded Gods of War coast with no units in the view and zero model commands throughout. The normal session supplies committed wind as the scene advances through ticks 31–210. The pair enables water and reflections together; the empty scene contains no reflected model or projectile subjects. Six seconds at 30 frames per second.

motion.label: An empty coast with wind-driven water and shoreline foam
motion.caption: Gods of War · empty coast · 6 seconds of normal wind-driven water.

features.title: A reflection beneath the hull.
features.intro: Faint, rippled reflections sit beneath boats and eligible projectiles.
features.original: The original water art and wake particles do not mirror above-water unit geometry.
features.how: Visible model faces and eligible projectiles feed a reflection layer clipped to the water. Physical height positions the reflection, while a cool tint, softening and wind-driven ripples keep it subtle. This is a screen-space approximation: hidden and off-screen surfaces are not reconstructed.
features.look: the faint mirrored loading deck and tall structure just below the transport. The broadside view exposes more reflection than the previous low cruiser.
features.capture: One ARM transport ship, armtship, replaces the previous two-ship scene. Its taller native geometry exposes more of the reflection, especially broadside. The ship receives normal movement orders; positions, heading, wind and COB wakes come from the simulation. Paired frames toggle only reflections, retaining other coastal effects. No opacity or model-height changes are made. The reflection becomes less exposed as the hull turns diagonally.

motion.label: A tall ARM transport ship with a reflection of its loading deck and crane
motion.caption: Gods of War · one tall ARM transport · reflections off / on.

features.title: Metal and paint catch the light.
features.intro: Broad metal highlights and softer painted surfaces respond as a unit turns.
features.original: Palette shading gives models their shape, without this extra directional specular highlight.
features.how: Recognized metal textures receive a broad, cool response beneath the directional glint. Painted panels receive a weaker, rougher highlight. Face orientation controls both, while the original panel colors and dark seams remain visible. Untagged textures keep their existing shading.
features.look: the broad sloping panels brightening and cooling as you rotate the unit toward the light. Switch the finish off and on at the same angle to separate the added response from the original shading.
features.capture: The live browser study uses a frozen, activated pose of the original ARM mobile Annihilator. Its metal and paint annotations, directional response, and glint formulas come from renderer revision 801c8b2. WebGL draws the model with a freely adjustable camera and a neutral backdrop; projection, depth testing, and antialiasing differ from the game. The optional light orbit rotates that normally fixed direction to study highlights on a stationary unit; Reset view restores the game’s light direction. The in-game comparison below retains the original paired 360° captures on Comet Catcher, switching materials and glints together at each recorded pose.

motion.label: An ARM mobile Annihilator rotates to show metal and paint finishes with directional glints
motion.caption: Original ARM mobile Annihilator · staged 360° rotation · materials + glints off / on.

features.title: Footsteps and tracks linger.
features.intro: Walking robots leave footprints. Tanks leave paired tracks.
features.original: Units cross the terrain without these persistent ground marks.
features.how: The modern renderer follows visible ground movement and places alternating footprints for walkers or paired segments for tracked units. Marks darken the existing terrain, remain beneath units and scenery, and fade over ten seconds of game time. They are visual traces; they do not change the terrain or reveal unseen movement.
features.look: the separate footsteps behind the ARM Hammer and the two continuous lines behind the Bulldog. Older marks fade as the units move away.
features.capture: An original ARM Hammer and Bulldog receive normal move orders across a prepared clearing on Comet Catcher. The original terrain remains; obstructing map features are removed before setup. Movement, poses and footprint/track placement then follow normal session steps and committed presentation updates. The 14-second capture lets the earliest marks fade. No trail artwork, positions or opacity are fabricated.

motion.label: An ARM Hammer and Bulldog cross open ground, leaving alternating footprints and parallel tank tracks that fade
motion.caption: Comet Catcher · ARM Hammer footsteps and Bulldog tracks · 14 seconds.
